word:hebrew:H1061.explanation: Bikkûwr means the first fruits of a crop—the earliest produce gathered from the land, such as the first fruits of wheat harvest.

word:hebrew:H1128.explanation: This Hebrew word is the personal name Ben, identifying a person in the Old Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than as a general description or action word. The name appears twice within the Hebrew Bible corpus, both in the same verse: 1 Kings 4:9. Since no broader definition or verse text is available here, its secure lexical role is to identify this individual. The surrounding passage is needed to explain the person’s particular place or responsibility in that verse.

word:hebrew:H1164.explanation: Bᵉʻî means a prayer and can also refer to the grave.

word:hebrew:H1263.explanation: Baruk is a personal name, rendered Baruch in English.

word:hebrew:H134.explanation: The word refers to “sockets,” functioning as a noun for structural pieces used in the tabernacle’s construction. It appears especially in Exodus, where it repeatedly identifies these supporting components in descriptions of the sanctuary and its court. The word occurs 57 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a focused meaning rather than a broad abstract idea. Its use is connected with making and setting these sockets in place. [Citations: Exod. 26:19; Exod. 27:10; Exod. 27:16; p03:word:hebrew:H134:event:canon:Exod:26:32:3]

word:hebrew:H1366.explanation: Gᵉbûwl means a boundary or border, marking the limit of a land or region.

word:hebrew:H1472.explanation: Geviyah means a body, whether alive or dead. It may refer to living bodies or to a dead animal’s carcass.

word:hebrew:H1498.explanation: Gazêl means robbery. It can also refer to plunder—something taken by violence.

word:hebrew:H1537.explanation: Gilgal is the name of three places in Palestine.

word:hebrew:H1595.explanation: Genez means a treasury. It can also refer to a chest.

word:hebrew:H1731.explanation: Duwd means a pot for boiling. It can also mean a basket.

word:hebrew:H178.explanation: Owb refers to a familiar spirit, one that people sought or consulted. It can also describe a necromancer.

word:hebrew:H1843.explanation: Dea means knowledge. It can also mean an opinion.

word:hebrew:H1906.explanation: This Hebrew word means “shouting,” referring to a loud vocal expression rather than a person, object, or action of movement. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Ezekiel 7:7. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence cannot be described beyond this basic lexical sense. Its role is to identify shouting in that occurrence.

word:hebrew:H192.explanation: Evil-Merodak is the name of a Babylonian king.

word:hebrew:H1991.explanation: This Hebrew word means “any,” serving to refer non-specifically to a person, thing, or amount rather than identifying one particular item. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, in Ezekiel 7:11. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its exact grammatical role in that sentence cannot be described further. Its basic force remains an indefinite reference: it points to something without specifying precisely which one.

word:hebrew:H2046.explanation: Hittûwk refers to melting or being melted.

word:hebrew:H206.explanation: Aven is a place name used for three places.

word:hebrew:H2190.explanation: This word is the personal name Zaavan. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears twice, once in Genesis 36:27 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:42. Both recorded English renderings preserve the name as Zaavan, so no broader ordinary meaning is established here beyond its use as a personal name. Its precise significance in either genealogy depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:hebrew:H2200.explanation: Zeiq means to make an outcry, or to cry out.

word:hebrew:H2239.explanation: Zereth means a span, a measure used for length or width.

word:hebrew:H2275.explanation: Chebron is a place name for Hebron in Palestine.

word:hebrew:H2352.explanation: Chuwr means a hole or crevice.

word:hebrew:H2550.explanation: Châmal means to have compassion or pity. It can also mean to spare.

word:hebrew:H2569.explanation: This word means “fifth,” identifying the position of something as number five in an ordered sequence. It functions as an ordinal number rather than naming an object, person, or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, at Genesis 47:26. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains a ranking or position in a series: the fifth one. This is the only recorded occurrence in the Hebrew corpus.

word:hebrew:H2604.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to an appeal for compassionate help—an asking for “mercy” or “supplication.” It describes a person turning to another with a humble request rather than making a demand. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Daniel: once rendered “mercy” and once “supplication.” Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its shared idea is a plea seeking gracious attention or relief.

word:hebrew:H2648.explanation: Chaphaz means to hurry away. It can also mean to tremble.

word:hebrew:H2741.explanation: Haruphite is a designation for a person identified by that name. In the Hebrew Old Testament, the word is rendered “Haruphite,” preserving it as a personal or group designation rather than translating it as an ordinary quality or action. It occurs twice in the Hebrew corpus, both within 1 Chronicles 12:5. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific identity or role cannot be described further.

word:hebrew:H2868.explanation: This Hebrew word means “glad.” It describes a person who is glad, expressing a positive state rather than naming an object, action, or place. In its only recorded occurrence in the Hebrew Bible, it functions as a word describing the person involved. The exact force in Daniel 6:23 depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic meaning remains “glad” there.

word:hebrew:H2882.explanation: Tebaliah is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Tebaliah.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Bible corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 26:11. As with many personal names, its broader significance is not established by the name alone; the surrounding passage is needed to explain the person’s role. The supported meaning is therefore the individual’s name, Tebaliah.

word:hebrew:H291.explanation: Ahian is a personal name, functioning as the name of an individual rather than as a word describing an object, action, or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 7:19, and is rendered “Ahian.” Because it is a proper name, its role is to identify a person; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s particular place or significance in the passage.

word:hebrew:H2936.explanation: Tanaph means to soil or defile.

word:hebrew:H3232.explanation: This Hebrew word is a personal name, referring to Imnah. It is rendered “Imnah” and occurs five times in the Old Testament, appearing in genealogical and family records. The word identifies a person and, in one passage, the family group associated with him. Its use is therefore a name rather than a general description or action word. The surrounding verse determines which family connection is being emphasized in each occurrence.

word:hebrew:H3294.explanation: Jarah is a personal name, rendered “Jarah,” referring to a person named in an Old Testament genealogy. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles 9:42. The surrounding evidence places the name in relationships involving birth or begetting, so its role is to identify an individual within a family line. The name itself does not provide a broader ordinary meaning beyond this personal designation.

word:hebrew:H3319.explanation: This Hebrew word means “finished,” describing something brought to completion. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra 6:15. As a predicate, it states that an action, work, or undertaking has reached its completed point rather than remaining in progress. The English rendering “finished” supports this basic sense, but the surrounding verse is needed to explain what was finished in that occurrence. Thus, its central idea is completion.

word:hebrew:H3320.explanation: Yatsab means to take a position and remain standing. It can also describe presenting oneself before Yahweh.

word:hebrew:H3355.explanation: Joktan is a personal name referring to an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament, rather than a common word describing an action or quality. It appears six times, consistently rendered “Joktan,” in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. The passages place the name within genealogical material, where it is connected with family descent and the listing of descendants. Its role is therefore to identify a person in these records.

word:hebrew:H3416.explanation: Irpeel is a Hebrew proper name preserved in English as “Irpeel.” It does not have an explicit definition or ordinary descriptive gloss in the available material, so its meaning is best treated as a name rather than translated as a common word. This Hebrew entity occurs once, in Joshua 18:27, and the same rendering appears in both listed English versions. Its precise referent belongs to that verse’s surrounding context.

word:hebrew:H343.explanation: Eid means misfortune or ruin, including calamity and destruction.

word:hebrew:H3481.explanation: This Hebrew word means “Israelite,” identifying a person as belonging to Israel. It functions as a designation for someone connected with the people of Israel, rather than naming a general action, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Leviticus 24:10 and once in 2 Samuel 17:25. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic meaning remains a person identified as an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H3562.explanation: Conaniah is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. It appears six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in three verses of 2 Chronicles. The English rendering is “Conaniah.” The available passages identify the person through relationships with others, but without the verse text, this word alone does not establish his role or significance in those events.

word:hebrew:H3588.explanation: Kiy is a linking word that can mean “that,” connecting one statement with what follows. It can also introduce a reason, meaning “because.”

word:hebrew:H3618.explanation: Kallah means a bride. It can also refer to a son's wife, or daughter-in-law.

word:hebrew:H3654.explanation: Kên means a gnat, rendered as lice in the passages describing the Egyptian plague. It can also mean manner.

word:hebrew:H3773.explanation: Kâruthâh means something cut, a hewn timber or beam.

word:hebrew:H3812.explanation: Leah is the name of Jacob’s wife.

word:hebrew:H3935.explanation: Laadah is a Hebrew personal name, functioning as the name of an individual rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:21, and is rendered “Laadah.” Because this name occurs only in a genealogy and no broader lexical definition is supplied, its ordinary meaning is its identifying use as a personal name. The name alone does not establish additional details about the person who bore it.

word:hebrew:H3940.explanation: Lappid means a torch or lamp, a burning source of light. For example, it describes lamps or torches placed inside pitchers.

policy.priorReviewerNotes: The lexical evidence supports both “haven” and “entry,” but Ezekiel 27:3 directly supports only the entry rendering, not the claim that the word means a haven such as an entry point. The sentence also combines distinct glosses into one non-atomic claim.

word:hebrew:H4062.explanation: This Hebrew word means “golden,” describing something associated with gold or having a gold-like quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 14:4, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. In that occurrence, it functions as part of the wording connected with the king of Babylon’s taunt. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its description of the king’s former oppression.

word:hebrew:H4088.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “Madmenah,” a named place. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 10:31, and the English renderings preserve it as a name rather than translating it into an ordinary descriptive word. Because it is a place name occurring in only one verse, its precise significance depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies Madmenah. It is connected there with other named locations and with movement or activity involving them.

word:hebrew:H4116.explanation: Māhar means to hurry or hasten, acting promptly.

word:hebrew:H413.explanation: El is a Hebrew connecting word that often means to or toward. It can also mark position under, as in waters gathered under the sky, or opposition, as in going against inhabitants.

word:hebrew:H4181.explanation: Morashah means a possession. It can describe land given as an inheritance or heritage.

word:hebrew:H4273.explanation: This Hebrew word is a rare term whose ordinary meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 30:26, and no explicit definition or approved meaning term is available here. Its precise sense therefore requires the verse text and broader surrounding context rather than a guessed translation. The word is identified as מַחַץ in the source record.

word:hebrew:H4318.explanation: Micah is a personal name used for Israelites.

word:hebrew:H4354.explanation: This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Numbers 26:29, within a genealogical setting. The surrounding evidence connects it with birth or begetting and genealogy, so it functions as a designation connected with a family line rather than as a broad everyday description. Its precise reference must be understood from the wording and names in that passage.

word:hebrew:H4471.explanation: This Hebrew word is a proper name: “Mamre.” It identifies a particular place in the Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. The name appears ten times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Genesis, and is consistently rendered “Mamre.” Its use is concentrated in passages connected with Abraham’s dwelling and the surrounding events recorded there. As a place-name, its precise significance in any individual verse comes from that verse’s surrounding context.

word:hebrew:H4619.explanation: Maaz is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Maaz” in English. It functions as a person’s designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs only once, at 1 Chronicles 2:27. No further lexical definition is available here, so its supported meaning is the name itself, not an inferred idea or translation beyond “Maaz.”

word:hebrew:H4655.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “escape”—a way of getting away from danger, pressure, or confinement. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 55:8. Because it occurs only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the wider context. Its basic sense is nevertheless clear: escape or a place of escape, expressing removal from a threatening situation.

policy.priorReviewerNotes: LEX_DEF supports the meaning, but W2 only lists Mikloth by name and does not directly support the claim that it was a place in the Desert.

word:hebrew:H4794.explanation: Merutsah means running—the act or progress of moving along. It can also mean a course.

policy.futureRepairGate: Reopen only after a verified source-alignment, lexical-identity, or evidence-view correction materially changes the closed evidence.
policy.priorReviewerNotes: Judges 5:11 directly supports a place of drawing water, but does not directly support the stated trough-for-cattle sense. The single claim combines both senses, so the Scripture evidence does not validate the full sentence.

word:hebrew:H4938.explanation: Mishenah means a walking stick or support.

word:hebrew:H5021.explanation: Nebushazban is a personal name appearing among the king of Babylon’s chief officers.

word:hebrew:H509.explanation: This Hebrew verb means “urged”: it describes pressing another person toward an action or response. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Judges 16:16, so its broader range cannot be established from repeated biblical uses of this word. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function is to express urging directed from one person toward another.

word:hebrew:H5115.explanation: Nava means to rest or stay at home. It can also describe preparing a habitation.

word:hebrew:H5159.explanation: Nachalah means an inheritance or heritage. It can also refer to a portion or possession, including land and cities received as an inheritance.

word:hebrew:H5160.explanation: This Hebrew word is the proper name “Nahaliel,” not a general description, action, or quality. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, with both occurrences in Numbers 21:19. The English renderings consistently preserve it as “Nahaliel,” indicating that it functions as a name rather than being translated into an ordinary meaning term. Its precise significance in the verse depends on the surrounding passage, but at the word level it identifies Nahaliel.¹

word:hebrew:H5223.explanation: Nakeh describes someone as maimed or lame. It can also describe a dejected or contrite spirit.

word:hebrew:H530.explanation: Emunah means firmness. It can also describe faithfulness.

word:hebrew:H545.explanation: This Hebrew word means “brought,” describing an action in which someone or something is moved or presented into a situation. It functions as an action word rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Esther 2:20. The precise force of the action depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense centers on being brought into a stated circumstance or setting.

word:hebrew:H5476.explanation: Sodi is a Hebrew personal name preserved in English as “Sodi.” It functions as a person’s name rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 13:10. The available form identifies the person by name, but does not provide a separate lexical definition or broader meaning for the name itself.

word:hebrew:H5542.explanation: Selah means a pause or musical suspension.

word:hebrew:H5627.explanation: Sara means apostasy or rebellion, describing a turning away from Yahweh and the way he commanded.

word:hebrew:H5685.explanation: ʻAbash means to dry up. It can also mean to be rotten, as with seed described as rotten.

word:hebrew:H5810.explanation: Azaz means to be stout, literally or figuratively. It can describe strengthening oneself. It can also describe prevailing over an opponent.

word:hebrew:H5865.explanation: This word means “ever”. It expresses an enduring span of time, pointing to what continues without a stated end. In its only Hebrew Old Testament occurrence, it is rendered “ever” in 2 Chronicles 33:7, but the verse text is not available here, so the surrounding context must determine the precise force of the word in that sentence. It functions as a time expression rather than naming a person, object, or action.

word:hebrew:H6006.explanation: ʻÂmas means to load or impose a burden. It describes a donkey being loaded and people being burdened with a yoke.

word:hebrew:H602.explanation: Anaq means to shriek. It can describe crying or groaning.

word:hebrew:H6091.explanation: Atsab means an idolatrous image, or idol.

word:hebrew:H6143.explanation: Iqqeshuth means perversity, or being froward and perverse.

word:hebrew:H6217.explanation: Ashuq means oppression or tyranny. It can also describe people who are oppressed.

word:hebrew:H6334.explanation: Poratha is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears only once, and its English rendering remains the name “Poratha.” Because no explicit definition or broader usage is available, the safest understanding is simply that Poratha identifies a person. Its precise role in Esther 9:8 depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

word:hebrew:H6378.explanation: Pak means a flask from which liquid may flow.

word:hebrew:H6402.explanation: This Hebrew word means "service," referring to work performed for a recognized purpose or responsibility. It functions as a noun, naming the service itself rather than describing an action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 7:19, so its broader range cannot be established from repeated uses. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is service offered in an assigned or meaningful role.

word:hebrew:H6583.explanation: Pashchûwr is a personal name used for Israelites.

word:hebrew:H6709.explanation: Tsachănâh means stench, an unpleasant smell.

word:hebrew:H6730.explanation: Zior is a Hebrew place-name, identifying a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Joshua 15:54. Because no explanatory definition or surrounding verse text is available here, its secure meaning is the proper name “Zior.” The name should therefore be read as a geographic designation in that passage, rather than translated as an ordinary descriptive word.

word:hebrew:H6745.explanation: This Hebrew word means “pans.” It names a concrete household object rather than a person, place, or abstract idea. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 2 Chronicles 35:13. In that verse, it functions as an object connected with an action involving food preparation, although the particular action and significance require the surrounding verse text. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: “pans,” referring to the objects themselves.

word:hebrew:H6828.explanation: Tsaphown means north, the northward direction.

word:hebrew:H6864.explanation: This Hebrew word means “flint,” referring to a stone used as an object. It occurs twice in the Old Testament corpus, once in Exodus 4:25 and once in Ezekiel 3:9. The rendering “flint” is the dominant supported meaning, so the word should be understood as naming this particular stone rather than as a broad term for any sharp object. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H6961.explanation: Qâveh means a measuring cord or line.

word:hebrew:H7038.explanation: This Hebrew word means “lacking.” It describes something as missing what is needed or expected, functioning as a description rather than naming a person or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Leviticus 22:23. Its use there is connected with describing an animal, but the verse text is needed to explain the specific force of the word in that passage.

word:hebrew:H7074.explanation: This Hebrew word identifies a person or people as a Kenizzite, also rendered “Kenezite” or “Kenizzite.” It functions as a group or ancestry designation rather than describing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs four times: once in Genesis, once in Numbers, and twice in Joshua. The word is especially connected with Caleb’s identification as a Kenizzite in Joshua, while its precise significance in each passage depends on the surrounding context.

word:hebrew:H7157.explanation: This Hebrew word is a place-name rendered “Jearim.” It identifies a specific location mentioned in Israel’s territorial and historical records rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The name appears 39 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 19 verses, especially in Joshua and Chronicles. Its repeated use in geographical lists and accounts of movement to or from the location helps readers recognize it as a fixed place-name. The precise significance of the location in any passage depends on that passage’s surrounding context.

word:hebrew:H7180.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “cucumbers,” the name of a food. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 11:5, so its normal lexical meaning is clear, while its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word functions as a concrete term for the food itself, rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea.

word:hebrew:H7203.explanation: Ro'eh means a seer, a person sought for inquiry of God. It can also mean a vision.

word:hebrew:H7351.explanation: Rechit means a panel resembling a trough; a verse renders it as “rafters.”

word:hebrew:H7412.explanation: Remah means to throw or cast. It can also mean to impose.

word:hebrew:H7535.explanation: Raq means only or merely, limiting what is being said. It can also mark an exception or a contrasting qualification, rendered as “except” or “yet” in different contexts.

word:hebrew:H7540.explanation: Raqad means to spring about. It can describe dancing or skipping.

word:hebrew:H7579.explanation: Shā'ab means to draw or bale up water.

word:hebrew:H7597.explanation: Shealtiel is the name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H7607.explanation: She'er refers to food and to close blood relatives.

word:hebrew:H783.explanation: Artachshasta means Artaxerxes, a title rather than a personal name, used for several Persian kings.

word:hebrew:H7881.explanation: Sîychah means reflection or meditation. It can also refer to devotion or prayer.

word:hebrew:H7962.explanation: Shalvah means security, whether genuine or false. It can also describe prosperity, abundance, peace, or quietness in biblical contexts.

word:hebrew:H7988.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to something associated with birth or begetting. Its recorded use is limited to one occurrence in the Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 28:57. There, it functions as an object in a passage connected with birth or begetting, so its precise reference depends on the verse’s wording and surrounding context. Scripture’s available connections place it within the setting of childbirth and family descent.

word:hebrew:H8004.explanation: Shâlêm is an early name for Jerusalem, appearing in English as Salem.

word:hebrew:H8141.explanation: Shâneh means a year, a cycle of time. In an age expression, it can mark how old someone is, as in “twenty years old.”

word:hebrew:H8325.explanation: Sharar is a Hebrew personal name, not a word whose ordinary meaning can be established from the available lexical information. It appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, at 2 Samuel 23:33, and English translations preserve it as “Sharar.” Because no explicit definition or broader usage is available, the safest understanding is simply the name of a person identified in that passage. Its precise significance depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:hebrew:H8350.explanation: Shashar means red ochre, a red pigment. It is used as red paint on a house and to color portrayed images red.

word:hebrew:H8369.explanation: Shethar is the name of a Persian satrap, listed among the princes of Persia and Media.

word:hebrew:H8387.explanation: This Hebrew word is the place name “Shiloh.” It refers to a geographic location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both within Joshua 16:6. Because no broader lexical definition is provided, its ordinary meaning is best understood as the name of that place. The surrounding verse context would be needed to explain its specific role in the boundary description, but the name itself identifies Shiloh.

word:hebrew:H8400.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to a “blemish,” serving as a label for an imperfection identified in the Old Testament. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, at Leviticus 21:20. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the wider context. Its basic meaning remains focused and specific: it identifies something regarded as a blemish rather than describing an action, person, or general condition.

word:hebrew:H8439.explanation: Tola is the name of two Israelites.

word:hebrew:H8475.explanation: Tahrea is a Hebrew personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 9:41, and is rendered “Tahrea.” Because no broader definition or contextual verse text is available here, the name itself should not be assigned an additional meaning. Its role is simply to identify the person named in that genealogical record.

word:hebrew:H8552.explanation: Tamam means to complete or finish something. It can describe something being spent. It can also describe something being consumed.

word:hebrew:H8646.explanation: This word is the personal name “Terah,” referring to a man in the Old Testament. It functions as a name rather than a general description or action. The surrounding genealogical records connect Terah with births, family relationships, and the movements of his household. The name occurs 13 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing mainly in Genesis and also in later genealogical records. Scripture also associates references to Terah with death, completing the account of his life within the biblical record.

word:hebrew:H866.explanation: Ethnah means a present given as the price of harlotry, or a reward.

word:hebrew:H963.explanation: This Hebrew word means “contempt.” It is a noun describing the condition of being treated with disdain or dishonor. In its single Old Testament occurrence, it refers to contempt connected with speech and the response to a king’s command. Its precise force in Esther 1:18 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains contempt directed toward a person or authority.
